en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Offenses Entailing Expiation (Pācittiyakaṇḍa)
The Chapter on the Naked Ascetics 46.
The Training Rule on Conduct.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Now at that time, a family that was the supporter of the Venerable Upananda the Sakyan son invited the Venerable Upananda the Sakyan son for a meal;
other monks were also invited for a meal.
On that occasion, the Venerable Upananda the Sakyan son was visiting families before the meal.
Then those bhikkhus said this to those people:
“Give us food, friends.
“Wait, venerable sirs, until the worthy Upananda arrives.”
A second time, those bhikkhus said this to those people:
“Give us food, friends; the time is passing. A third time, those bhikkhus said this to those people:
“Give us food, friends; the time is passing.”
“Venerable sir, we have prepared this meal for the sake of the noble Upananda.
Please wait, venerable sir, until the noble Upananda arrives.
Then the Venerable Upananda the Sakyan son, having visited families before the meal, arrived at midday.
The monks did not eat according to their own preference.
Those monks who were of few desires... [as before] ...were indignant, complained, and spread it about, saying:
"How can the venerable Upananda the Sakyan son, having been invited for a communal meal, go on a visit among families before the meal?"... [as before] ...
“Is it true, Upananda, that even though you have been invited for a meal and have already received food, you still go on a visit to families before the meal?
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked him... [as before]...
"How indeed, foolish man, can you, having been invited and being provided with a meal, go on a visit among families before the meal?
This, foolish man, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule thus:"
“Whatever monk, having been invited and having accepted a meal, should go on a visit to families before the meal, there is an offense of expiation.
Thus was this training rule laid down by the Blessed One for the monks.
Now at that time, a family that was the supporter of the Venerable Upananda the Sakyan sent hard food for the Saṅgha.
“Having shown it to the Venerable Upananda, it should be given to the Saṅgha.
Now at that time, the Venerable Upananda the Sakyaputta had entered the village for alms.
Then those people went to the monastery and asked the bhikkhus:
“Venerable sir, where is the noble Upananda?
“Friend, that venerable Upananda, son of the Sakyans, has entered the village for alms.
“Venerable sir, having shown this fresh food to the noble Upananda, it should be given to the Saṅgha.”
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, having given a discourse on the Dhamma with reference to this cause and this context, addressed the bhikkhus:
“In that case, bhikkhus, accept it and set it aside until Upananda arrives.”

Then the Venerable Upananda the Sakyaputta, thinking, “The Blessed One has prohibited visiting families before the meal,” visited families after the meal and returned during the day; consequently, the fresh food was left over.

Those monks who were of few desires... [as before]... complained, grumbled, and became indignant, saying, “How can the Venerable Upananda the Sakyaputta visit families after the meal?”... [as before]...
“Is it true, Upananda, that you go on visits to families after the meal?
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked him... [as before]...
"How indeed, foolish man, can you go on a visit among families after the meal?
This, foolish man, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule as follows:"
“Now, whatever bhikkhu, having been invited and having partaken of a meal, should visit families either before the meal or after the meal, it is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
Thus was this training rule laid down by the Blessed One for the bhikkhus.
At that time, however, the bhikkhus, being scrupulous, did not visit families during the period for the distribution of robes.
A small amount of robe-cloth arose.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
… “Monks, I allow you to visit families at the time of giving robe-cloth.”
And thus, monks, you should recite this training rule:
“Whatever monk, having been invited and being provided with a meal, should go on a visit among families before the meal or after the meal, except at the proper time, there is an offense of expiation.
Herein, this is the proper time: the time for giving robes—this is the proper time therein.”
Thus was this training rule laid down by the Blessed One for the monks.
Now at that time, the monks were engaged in robe-making, and there was need for needles, thread, and knives.
Being afraid of wrongdoing, the monks did not visit families.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One...
[as before] ... "I allow you, monks, to visit families at the time of making robes.

And thus, monks, you should recite this training rule: ‘If a monk, when it is not the time for making robes, should visit families for the purpose of robe-making, he commits an offense of wrong-doing.’"

“Whatever monk, having been invited to a meal and having accepted it, should visit families before the meal or after the meal, except on an appropriate occasion, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
Herein, this is the appropriate occasion: the time for giving robes, the time for making robes—this is the appropriate occasion therein.
Thus was this training rule laid down by the Blessed One for the monks.
Now at that time, the monks were ill and there was need for medicines.
Being afraid of wrongdoing, the monks did not visit families.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One... [as before]...
“I allow you, monks, to visit families after having asked permission from a monk who is present.
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule as follows:

‘If a monk, having been invited and being provided with a meal, should visit families before or after the meal without asking permission from a monk who is present, except on an appropriate occasion, it is an offense entailing confession (pācittiya).’”
In this regard, this is the occasion: the time for giving robes and the time for making robes—this is the occasion therein.
“But whoever,” means whoever of such a kind... [and so forth].
"Bhikkhu" ...
[as before] ... this is the "bhikkhu" intended in this context.
"Invited" means:
"Invited to one of the five kinds of cooked food":
"eaten together" means that he has eaten with the very person by whom he was invited.
It is possible to enter after having requested permission from a monk who is present;
it is not possible [to do so] from a monk who is absent.
It is not possible to enter after having taken leave.
"Before the meal" means one who has not yet eaten that for which he was invited.
"After the meal" means that at least as much as the tip of a blade of kusa grass has been eaten by the one who was invited.
"Family" means:
There are four classes: the khattiya class, the brāhmaṇa class, the vessa class, and the sudda class.
"One should enter among the families" means that for one who enters the vicinity of another's house, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
When he steps over the threshold with the first foot, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
When he steps over the second foot, there is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
Except on an appropriate occasion.
Except on special occasions.
A "robe-giving occasion" refers to the last month of the rainy season when the kaṭhina has not been spread, or the five months when the kaṭhina has been spread.
The "robe-making time" refers to when a robe is being made. If a monk,

having been invited and perceiving himself as invited, goes among families before or after the meal without having asked permission from a monk who is present— except on an appropriate occasion— he commits an offense of expiation (pācittiya).

If a monk who has been invited, being in doubt, goes among families before or after a meal without having asked permission from a monk who is present, except on an appropriate occasion, he commits an offense entailing confession (pācittiya).

If a monk who has been invited, perceiving himself as not invited, goes among families before or after a meal without having asked permission from a monk who is present, except on an appropriate occasion, he commits an offense entailing confession.
If a monk who has not been invited, perceiving himself as invited, [goes among families], he commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one summons while being doubtful, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one summons while perceiving that one has not been summoned, there is no offense.
There is no offense—
At the proper time,
he enters after having asked permission of a monk who is present,
and he enters without asking permission of a monk who is absent.
The path goes through another's house;
the path goes along the vicinity of a house;
he goes into the middle of a monastery.
She goes to a nunnery,
she goes to the lodgings of non-Buddhist ascetics,
she goes to a place for returning.
Going to a house of devotion,
in times of misfortune,
[and] for one who is insane.
"For one who is a first-offender.
The sixth training rule on conduct is finished.
